title: Steak and Kidney Pudding
subtitle: Suet pastry, beef and kidney, steamed for four hours
excerpt: The definitive British steamed pudding: chuck steak and ox kidney in a rich gravy, enclosed in a suet-crust pastry and steamed for four hours until the pastry is fluffy and the filling yields to a spoon. No other dish quite like it.

recipe.sourceNotes: The steamed suet pudding is one of the few genuinely British contributions to the world's culinary canon, with no direct equivalent in other cuisines. Steak and kidney pudding, as distinct from the baked pie, was codified in Victorian cooking and became one of the signature dishes of Alexis Soyer, the celebrated chef at the Reform Club who adapted it for public catering in the 1840s. The suet pastry that lines and caps the pudding basin is quite different from the shortcrust used for pies: shredded suet produces a light, open, almost dumpling-like texture after long steaming. The filling is traditionally raw rather than pre-cooked, so it braises inside the pastry in its own juices over the four-hour steam. The result is a pudding that collapses with richness when turned out.

recipeTools.notes: A large saucepan deep enough to hold the pudding basin on a trivet with the lid on.

content.text: The suet pastry should be soft and pliable, not dry: add more cold water a tablespoon at a time if it crumbles. Line the basin right to the top and leave a generous overhang. The paper-and-foil lid must be pleated across the middle to allow for expansion as the pudding rises. Keep the water in the steaming pan at a steady simmer; if it stops, the pudding stalls. Top up with boiling water from a kettle every 45 minutes.

items.preparation: trimmed and cut into 1.5 cm pieces

content.text: Make the suet pastry: mix the self-raising flour, suet, and salt in a bowl. Add about 100 to 120 ml of cold water, a little at a time, until a soft dough forms. Knead briefly until smooth. Set aside a quarter of the pastry for the lid and roll the rest into a circle large enough to line a buttered 1.2-litre pudding basin with a 2 cm overhang.

Toss the beef and kidney in the seasoned flour. Mix with the chopped onion, Worcestershire sauce, and thyme sprigs. Pack into the lined basin. Pour over the stock. The basin should be about three-quarters full.

Roll the reserved pastry into a circle to fit the top. Lay it over the filling and pinch the edges together firmly to seal. Cover the top of the basin with a double layer of greaseproof paper and then foil, both pleated across the middle. Tie securely with string, leaving a handle for lifting.

Place the basin on a trivet or upturned saucer in a large saucepan. Add enough boiling water to come halfway up the side of the basin. Cover tightly and steam over medium-low heat for 4 to 4.5 hours, topping up with boiling water as needed. The pudding is ready when the pastry has puffed and firmed. Turn out onto a deep plate to serve.
